expert_workflow: 1. Scan through each ingredient, categorize them into macronutrient groups (e.g., chicken = protein).
2. Select ingredients that are within the group specified in the goal (e.g., protein).

3. Assess whether the ingredients specified in the meal description align with the version of the macronutrient (lean, low fat, etc.). Use the USDA nutritional database as a reference. (e.g., “chicken breast” is lean protein, “chicken leg” is not lean protein).
5. Assess for cooking method (roasting versus frying).
6. Estimate the contribution of this ingredient to the overall meal (if this is cheese in a salad, even though it is not low-fat, it may not contribute too much to the meal overall).

7. If the ingredients in the specified macronutrient group/food group align with the version described in the goal (lean, low fat, whole grain, etc.), and there is a low contribution from hidden ingredients and cooking method, the meal meets the goal; otherwise, the meal does not meet the goal.
1. Scan through the ingredients, categorizing them into macronutrient/food groups (e.g., fruits and vegetables, non-starchy vegetables, whole grains, etc.).
2. Select ingredients/food groups that align with the macronutrient/food group stated in the goal.

3. Estimate portion sizes of those ingredients (if not available in the description). Use typical portion sizes used in similar meals. Use references (databases) to find the nutritional content of specified ingredients, given their estimated portion sizes.
4. Combine all the portion sizes calculated in step 3 to arrive at the total amount of the macronutrient/food group specified in the goal.
5. Compare the calculated amount with the amount specified in the goal.
6. If the amount aligns with the goal, the meal meets the goal; if it does not, the meal does not meet the goal.
